topics.p: Can {{name}} find the contents page or index in a non-fiction book and use it to locate specific information — and do they understand why the author included those features?

topics.ds: Identify characters, settings, and major events in stories; become familiar with key stories, fairy tales, and traditional tales and retell them with key details in sequence
e: Name the main characters in a story
Describe where and when a story takes place
Retell a familiar story including beginning, middle, and end events
topics.p: After reading a fairy tale or story together, can {{name}} retell it to you in order — saying who was in it, where it happened, and what the main events were?

topics.ds: Compare and contrast the adventures and experiences of characters in familiar stories; identify similarities and differences between two texts on the same topic
e: Identify what two stories have in common (e.g. 'Both have a bear character')
Compare information from two books about the same topic
Discuss how characters' experiences are similar or different across stories
topics.p: If {{name}} has read two stories with similar themes — like two tales about a brave hero — can they tell you what was the same and what was different between them?

topics.ds: Link what is read or heard to own experiences; draw on background knowledge and vocabulary to support understanding of texts
e: Make text-to-self connections (e.g. 'This reminds me of when I...')
Use personal experience to understand a character's feelings
Relate events in a story to own life to deepen comprehension
topics.p: When {{name}} hears or reads a story about something familiar — like going to school or visiting a grandparent — do they connect it to their own life and use that to help understand what's happening?

topics.ds: Recognise common types of texts (storybooks, poems, non-fiction); name the author and illustrator and define the role of each in telling or presenting a text
e: Distinguish between a story, a poem, and a non-fiction book
Point to and name the author and illustrator on the cover
Explain that the author writes the words and the illustrator makes the pictures
topics.p: When you hand {{name}} a book, can they tell you whether it's a story or a fact book — and point out the author's name on the cover?

topics.ds: Participate in discussions about what is read, taking turns and listening to others; explain understanding clearly; actively engage in group reading activities
e: Share ideas about a book in a group discussion
Listen to and respond to others' opinions about a text
Take turns speaking and build on what classmates have said about a book
topics.p: When {{name}}'s class discusses a book they've all read, does {{name}} join in — sharing their own ideas and listening to what others think, even if their view is different?

topics.ds: Listen to and discuss poems, stories, and non-fiction at a level beyond independent reading; confirm understanding of texts read aloud by asking and answering questions about key details
e: Answer questions about a story or non-fiction text read aloud by the teacher
Discuss events, characters, or ideas from chapter books read to the class
Ask for clarification when something in a read-aloud is not understood
topics.p: After you read a story aloud to {{name}}, can they answer questions about what happened — like who the main character was, where the story took place, and what the problem was?

topics.ds: Identify the main topic and retell key details of informational texts; describe connections between individuals, events, ideas, or pieces of information
e: State what a non-fiction text is mostly about in one sentence
List two or three important facts learned from an informational text
Explain how two events or ideas in a text are connected
topics.p: After {{name}} reads a short fact book — like one about animals or space — can they tell you what the main topic was and give you a few key facts they learned from it?

topics.ds: Describe the relationship between illustrations and the text in which they appear; use pictures to support and extend comprehension
e: Use pictures to predict or confirm story events
Describe what is happening in an illustration and how it relates to the text
Explain how an illustration adds information not stated in words
topics.p: When {{name}} is reading a picture book, do they look at the illustrations to help them understand what's happening in the story — and can they explain how a picture connects to the words on the page?

topics.ds: Explore and compare how images contribute to meaning in different types of texts: illustrations that show characters and events in stories, and photographs, labelled diagrams and captions that give facts in informative texts
e: Point to a photo in an information book about frogs and say what fact it shows that the words do not
Listen to or read a caption or label beside a picture and explain what it adds
Compare an illustration of a bear in a story with a photo of a real bear in an information book and explain how each helps the reader differently
topics.p: When reading a book about animals with {{name}}, can they tell you what a photo or label shows — and how it's different from the drawings in a storybook?

topics.ds: Use visualising (making pictures in the mind from the words) and simple summarising to understand texts listened to, viewed or read: picturing what the words describe and telling what a text was mostly about
e: Close eyes during a read-aloud, then draw what they pictured and point to a word that helped
Describe what they 'see' in their head when they hear a sentence such as 'a huge, muddy puddle'
Tell in one or two sentences what a story or short video was mostly about
topics.p: When you read {{name}} a story without showing the pictures, can they describe or draw what they imagined — and tell you in a sentence what it was mostly about?

topics.ds: Ask and answer questions about key details in literary and informational texts; make simple inferences based on what characters say and do
e: Answer 'who', 'what', 'where' questions about a text using evidence
Infer a character's feelings from their actions (e.g. 'She's sad because she's crying')
Make logical guesses about unstated information using text clues
topics.p: While reading a story, can {{name}} answer questions like "Why did the character do that?" or "How do you think they felt?" — using clues from the text rather than just guessing?

topics.ds: Understand the conventions of simple digital texts: swiping or tapping arrows to turn pages, scrolling, using home and back icons, and reading screen text top to bottom and left to right as in print
e: Swipe or tap the arrow to move to the next page of a digital picture book
Scroll down a simple screen text and point to where to start reading
Tap the home or back icon to return to the start of a story app and explain what the icon does
topics.p: When {{name}} uses a story app on a tablet, can they swipe to turn the page, scroll down, and use the back or home button to find their way?

topics.ds: Retell stories including key details in sequence, describe characters, settings, and major events using evidence from the text, and describe the overall structure of a story (beginning, middle, ending)
e: Retell a familiar story in order, including at least three key details from beginning, middle, and end
Describe a character's appearance, actions, or personality using details from the text
Explain how the beginning of a story introduces the characters and setting, and how the ending concludes the action
topics.p: After reading a story, can {{name}} describe the main character — including what kind of person they are, what they wanted, and how they felt at the end — using details from the book?

topics.ds: Explore and replicate the rhythms and sound patterns of nursery rhymes, chants and songs by clapping or tapping the beat and joining in with repeated sound patterns
e: Clap the steady beat while saying a nursery rhyme such as 'Hickory Dickory Dock'
Repeat a chant line keeping the same rhythm the teacher used
Join in a song's repeated sound pattern (e.g. 'splish, splash') at the right moment
topics.p: When you sing or say a nursery rhyme together, can {{name}} clap along to the beat and join in with the repeated sounds?

topics.ds: Check that text makes sense while reading and self-correct inaccurate reading by re-reading or using context
e: Notice when reading does not make sense and stop to re-read
Self-correct errors mid-sentence (e.g. 'Wait, that doesn't sound right')
Use meaning, sentence structure, and visual cues together to monitor reading
topics.p: When {{name}} is reading and something doesn't quite make sense, do they go back and re-read that part — or use the surrounding words to work out what a tricky word or sentence means?

topics.ds: Share ideas about stories, poems and images by First Nations Australian, other Australian and world authors and illustrators, reflecting on experiences that are similar to or different from their own
e: Listen to a picture book by a First Nations Australian author, such as 'Welcome to Country' by Aunty Joy Murphy and Lisa Kennedy, and share one idea about what it shows
Say how a character's experience in an Australian story (e.g. Mem Fox's 'Possum Magic') is like or different from their own life
Respond to an illustration or short poem by saying what they notice and how it makes them feel
topics.p: After hearing a picture book by an Australian or First Nations author, does {{name}} share what they thought — like how a character's life is the same as or different from theirs?

topics.ds: Understand that texts come in many forms — signs, labels, books, cards and digital texts on tablets or screens — and that each carries a message to be read
e: Point to a STOP sign, an exit sign and a food label and say what message each gives
Sort a picture book, a road sign, a birthday card and a story app on a tablet into a group called 'texts'
Name a text they see on a screen at home or school (e.g. a game menu or video title) and say what it tells them
topics.p: When you're out walking, does {{name}} point to signs like STOP or the toilet sign and understand they are 'texts' with a message, just like books?

topics.ds: Identify familiar texts such as stories, information books, lists and recipes and say their purpose: to entertain, to give information or to tell us what to do
e: Say that a storybook is for enjoying a story and an animal fact book is for finding out facts
Explain what a shopping list or recipe is used for
Choose which book to use to find out what koalas eat and explain why
topics.p: If {{name}} wants to find out what koalas eat, do they know to pick an information book rather than a storybook — and can they say what each kind of book is for?

topics.ds: Discuss how authors' words and illustrators' images create characters, settings and events in literature by First Nations Australian, other Australian and world authors and illustrators
e: Point to words and pictures that show what a character is like in a book by a First Nations Australian author or illustrator (e.g. Gregg Dreise's 'Kookoo Kookaburra')
Explain how an illustrator shows an Australian setting (e.g. the colours and landscape in Bronwyn Bancroft's illustrations) and what the words add
Compare how a character is created in an Australian story (e.g. Pamela Allen's 'Who Sank the Boat?') and in a story by a world author
topics.p: When reading an Australian picture book, can {{name}} point to the words and pictures that show what a character or place is like?

topics.ds: Identify and compare characters' points of view, recognise who is narrating a story, describe how characters respond to events and challenges, and compare characters' experiences across different stories or versions of the same story
e: Identify who is telling a story and explain how you know (e.g. 'The wolf is telling the story because he says I')
Describe how a character responds to a problem or challenge using evidence from the text (e.g. 'When the bridge broke, she decided to swim across')
Compare how two characters from different stories react to a similar situation (e.g. how two heroes show bravery in different ways)
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a story told from one character's point of view, can they think about how a different character in the same story might have seen events differently?

topics.ds: Recognise recurring literary language in stories and poetry, identify words and phrases that suggest feelings or appeal to the senses, and discuss favourite words and phrases
e: Spot recurring story language such as 'Once upon a time' and 'happily ever after'
Identify sensory words and phrases in a poem: 'the icy wind howled'
Share a favourite word or phrase from a story and explain why it appeals
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a poem or a story with vivid language, can they pick out a phrase they really liked — and tell you why it works well or how it made them feel?

topics.ds: Explore how texts are organised in stages according to purpose: a recount (orientation, events in order, personal comment), a report (topic opener, facts grouped by feature) and a simple explanation (what happens and why, in steps)
e: Point to the 'who, where, when' opening, the events in order and the ending comment in a class recount of an excursion
Sort facts about penguins into groups (what they look like, what they eat, where they live) to show how a report is organised
Order picture cards for a simple explanation (e.g. how a seed grows into a plant) and say why the order matters
topics.p: After a family outing, can {{name}} tell you about it in order — who was there, what happened first, next and last — and finish with what they thought of it?

topics.ds: Identify the main topic of a multi-paragraph informational text, determine the focus of specific paragraphs, and explain how key details support the main idea
e: Identify the main topic of a multi-paragraph informational text and state the focus of individual paragraphs
Describe how specific details and facts in the text support the main idea
Explain how events, ideas, or steps in a text are connected (e.g. cause-effect, sequence, comparison)
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a multi-page article — like a school text about a historical event — can they tell you the main idea and then explain what each section was specifically about?

topics.ds: Use visualising as a comprehension strategy when listening, viewing and reading: building and revising a mental picture from descriptive words to support literal and inferred meaning
e: Sketch the picture they formed after hearing a descriptive passage without illustrations, and label it with words from the text
Describe what they see, hear and feel in their mind during a read-aloud of a storm scene
Watch a short animated version of a story they have heard, compare it with their mental picture, and revise what they infer (e.g. 'Now I see her crying, so she is upset')
topics.p: When reading a chapter book with no pictures, can {{name}} describe or draw the picture in their head — and change it when new details come up?

topics.ds: Navigate print and screen texts using chapters, tables of contents, indexes, side-bar menus, drop-down menus and links to find information
e: Use a side-bar menu on a children's website (e.g. a zoo or museum site) to find the page about a chosen animal
Open a drop-down menu and choose the right option to reach a section, then return to the home page
Find the same fact once with a book's index and once by following links on a website, and say which was quicker
topics.p: When looking something up on a kids' website, can {{name}} use the menu down the side or a drop-down list, and click links to find what they need?

topics.ds: Understand how screen texts are organised and navigated using navigation buttons, swipe screens, links, images and voice commands, alongside print features such as page numbers, contents and headings
e: Tap a navigation button or link in a children's e-book or website to go to a chosen page and back again
Use a voice command on a tablet or smart speaker (e.g. 'Read the next page') and say what happened
Compare finding a chapter with a print contents page and with a menu button in an app
topics.p: When using a kids' website or e-book, can {{name}} tap the buttons or links to find what they want — and get back to where they started?

topics.ds: Recognise different non-fiction text structures and features (headings, contents, glossary, index), understanding how texts are organised to present information
e: Use a contents page to find information on a specific topic in a non-fiction book
Identify the purpose of headings, glossary, and index in an information text
Recognise that non-fiction books can be structured as lists, time order, or question-and-answer
topics.p: When {{name}} is using a non-fiction book for a school project, do they know how to use the headings, contents page, and index to find what they need quickly?

topics.ds: Describe similarities and differences between imaginative, informative and persuasive texts, including simple persuasive texts such as posters, ads and letters that try to get the reader to do or think something
e: Sort a storybook, a fact book and a poster saying 'Come to our school fair!' into imaginative, informative and persuasive
Point to words in a simple ad or poster that try to convince the reader (e.g. 'best', 'you will love it')
Say one way a persuasive poster is like an information book and one way it is different
topics.p: When {{name}} sees a toy ad or a poster for an event, can they tell it's trying to convince them — and how that's different from a storybook or a fact book?

topics.ds: Discuss the sequence of events in narrative texts and how items of information are related in non-fiction, retelling stories including key details and demonstrating understanding of central message or lesson
e: Retell a story in correct sequence with beginning, middle, and end
Identify the central message or lesson of a story
Explain how two pieces of information in a non-fiction text are connected
topics.p: After {{name}} finishes a chapter book, can they explain the beginning, middle, and end in their own words — and describe what the story was really about at its heart?

topics.ds: Explore how repeated lines, rhyming words and a steady rhythm link the parts of simple poems, chants and songs so that they hang together (cohesion) and are easy to remember
e: Point to the line that repeats in a chant (e.g. 'We're going on a bear hunt') and say how it ties the verses together
Find the rhyming words at the ends of lines in a short poem and explain how they connect the lines
Clap the rhythm of two verses of a song and notice that the beat stays the same in each verse
topics.p: When {{name}} sings a favourite song or chant, do they notice the line that keeps repeating and the rhyming words that make it easy to remember?

topics.ds: Recognise different forms of poetry (free verse, narrative poetry, haiku) and discuss their features; prepare poems and play scripts to read aloud and perform with understanding through intonation, tone, volume and action
e: Name at least two different forms of poetry and describe a feature of each (e.g., 'narrative poetry tells a story', 'free verse does not have a regular rhyme or rhythm')
Recognise the form of a given poem and explain how you identified it (e.g., 'This is a narrative poem because it has characters and a plot')
Prepare and perform a poem or play script extract showing understanding through changes in intonation, volume, and expression
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a poem aloud, do they change their voice to match the mood — reading excitedly for a lively poem or quietly for a sad one — rather than reading it flat?

topics.ds: Discuss how characters and settings are connected in literature by First Nations Australian, other Australian and world authors and illustrators — how a place shapes what characters do and feel, and how characters belong to or change a place
e: Explain how Country and the characters are connected in a First Nations Australian picture book (e.g. 'Somebody's Land' by Adam Goodes, Ellie Laing and David Hardy)
Describe how the setting affects what a character does in an Australian story (e.g. the rainforest in Jeannie Baker's 'Where the Forest Meets the Sea')
Predict how a character from a world story would act if moved to a different setting, and give a reason
topics.p: When reading a story set in the Australian bush or by the sea, can {{name}} explain how the place affects what the characters do or feel?

topics.ds: Identify and describe how texts across the curriculum — such as science procedures, maths word problems, history recounts and health posters — are organised differently and use language features suited to their purposes
e: Point out the goal, materials list and numbered steps with command verbs in a science procedure
Compare a history recount's time words (first, in 1900, later) with an information report's headings and present-tense facts
Explain why a maths word problem ends with a question and a health poster uses short commands and pictures
topics.p: When {{name}} does homework, do they notice that a science experiment sheet, a maths word problem and a history story are set out differently — and why?

topics.ds: Draw inferences from independently-read texts, such as inferring characters' feelings, thoughts and motives from their actions, and justifying inferences with evidence from the text
e: Infer a character's feelings or motives from their actions and dialogue (e.g. 'She slammed the door — how is she feeling?')
Justify an inference by quoting or pointing to specific evidence in the text
Distinguish between what is explicitly stated and what must be inferred from clues in the text
topics.p: After {{name}} reads a chapter of a novel, can they explain how a character was feeling and why — pointing to something the character said or did as their evidence?

topics.ds: Identify main ideas drawn from more than one paragraph and summarise them; retrieve and record information from non-fiction texts using notes, tables or other methods
e: Read a multi-paragraph non-fiction text and state the main idea of each paragraph in one sentence
Summarise a text of 3+ paragraphs in 2-3 sentences capturing the key points
Retrieve specific information from a non-fiction text and record it using a simple table or notes (e.g., 'Name: hedgehog, Habitat: woodland, Diet: insects')
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a long non-fiction article or chapter, can they pull out the most important points and write them as a short summary — rather than just copying chunks of text?

topics.ds: Identify how similar topics and information are presented in different types of texts, such as a poem, an information report, a website and a picture book about the same subject
e: Compare a poem about the ocean with an information report about the ocean and say what each tells and how
Find the same fact about frogs on a website and in a book and describe how each presents it (e.g. video, photo, heading)
Explain why a picture book and a fact sheet about bees might be written differently
topics.p: If {{name}} reads a poem and a fact book about the same thing — say, the ocean — can they tell you how each one shares information differently?

topics.ds: Determine the central message, lesson, or moral of a story, fable, or folktale, explaining what the story teaches the reader and supporting the interpretation with key details from the text
e: State the lesson or moral of a fable in one sentence (e.g. 'The Tortoise and the Hare teaches that slow and steady wins the race')
Explain what a story's central message is using at least two details from the text as support
Distinguish the central message from a summary of events — explain what the story means, not just what happens
topics.p: After reading a fable like "The Tortoise and the Hare", can {{name}} tell you the lesson the story is teaching — and point to a moment in the story that shows that lesson?

topics.ds: Identify how language choices, text structure and presentational features (illustrations, diagrams, bold print, layout) contribute to the overall meaning and effect of a text
e: Explain how an author's word choices create a particular effect (e.g., 'The author uses "crept" instead of "walked" to make it feel sneaky and tense')
Identify how a text's structure helps the reader (e.g., 'The headings help you find information quickly', 'The story builds suspense before the ending')
Explain how a presentational feature contributes to meaning (e.g., 'The bold words are important vocabulary', 'The diagram shows how the water cycle works')
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a page with headings, diagrams, or bold words, can they explain how those features help — like "the diagram shows the water cycle because the words alone are hard to picture"?

topics.ds: Identify recurring themes (good vs evil, friendship, bravery) and conventions (once upon a time, moral at the end, hero's journey) across a wide range of books including fairy stories, myths, legends and traditional tales
e: Identify a common theme across two different stories (e.g., 'Both "Jack and the Beanstalk" and "The Three Billy Goats Gruff" are about bravery overcoming a threat')
Name literary conventions found in fairy tales and myths (e.g., 'once upon a time', magical numbers like three, a quest or journey, good triumphing over evil)
Explain how the same theme can appear in different genres (e.g., friendship in a realistic story vs a myth)
topics.p: After reading a few different fairy tales or myths, can {{name}} spot patterns — like "the hero always faces three challenges" or "good always wins in the end" — across the different stories?

topics.ds: Identify the purpose and intended audience of imaginative, informative and persuasive texts, using clues such as topic, words, pictures and where the text appears
e: Say who a text is mainly for (e.g. a toddler's board book, a school newsletter for parents, a cereal ad for children) and point to a clue
Identify the purpose and audience of a school fair poster
Explain how a book about dinosaurs for 4-year-olds is different from one for 10-year-olds
topics.p: When {{name}} sees a school newsletter, a toddler's book or a toy ad, can they say who it's meant for and point to a clue?

topics.ds: Distinguish one's own point of view from that of the author of an informational text and identify the author's purpose
e: Read an opinion article and state the author's point of view, then state one's own and explain how they differ
Identify whether an author's purpose is to inform, persuade, or entertain, citing evidence from the text
Explain how word choices in an informational text reveal the author's attitude toward the topic
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a fact book or an article, can they tell you what the author's purpose was — like whether they were trying to inform, persuade, or entertain — and whether they agree with the author's viewpoint?

topics.ds: Discuss characters and settings across a range of texts and identify how language — adjectives, verbs, dialogue and descriptive phrases — presents them in different ways
e: Find the words that show a character is grumpy in one story and cheerful in another (e.g. 'stomped', 'grumbled' vs 'skipped', 'giggled')
Compare how two texts describe a beach setting and list the descriptive words each uses
Explain how what a character says (dialogue) tells the reader what they are like
topics.p: Can {{name}} point to the words in a story that show a character is grumpy or kind — like 'stomped' or 'giggled'?

topics.ds: Analyse character traits, motivations, and feelings using text evidence, and distinguish one's own point of view from that of the narrator or characters
e: Identify two character traits from a story and cite the specific actions or dialogue that reveal each trait
Explain why a character made a particular decision by linking their motivation to events in the text
Describe where one's own opinion about a character differs from the narrator's portrayal and explain why
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a story, can they describe why a character made a particular choice — explaining their motivations — and also say whether they personally agree with what the character did?

topics.ds: Identify the audience and purpose of imaginative, informative and persuasive texts through their use of language features and images
e: Identify the audience of a picture book from its illustrations, font and vocabulary
Explain how the image and slogan on a healthy-eating poster show its purpose and audience
Point to the language features (e.g. facts and headings, or exclamations and 'you') that show whether a text informs or persuades
topics.p: When {{name}} looks at a poster or ad, can they use the pictures and words to tell who it's for and what it's trying to do?

topics.ds: Integrate information from two texts on the same topic in order to write or speak about the subject knowledgeably, combining and comparing what each source contributes
e: Read two informational texts on the same topic and identify information that appears in both, information unique to each, and any contradictions between them
Combine key details from two sources into a coherent summary or short report that draws on both texts
Explain how reading a second text on the same topic added to, confirmed, or challenged understanding gained from the first text
topics.p: If {{name}} is researching a topic using two different books or articles, can they combine the information they've gathered from both to talk or write about the subject more fully than either source alone?

topics.ds: Describe connections between events, ideas, or concepts in informational text using time, sequence, cause-and-effect, and comparison language, and identify logical connections between sentences and paragraphs
e: Read a science text and identify three cause-and-effect relationships using signal words like 'because', 'as a result'
Explain the sequence of steps in a technical procedure using time-order language ('first', 'next', 'finally')
Describe how two paragraphs in a text are connected (e.g. comparison, cause/effect, or sequence)
topics.p: After reading a non-fiction passage — like one about climate or history — can {{name}} explain what caused something to happen, what the effect was, and how the author linked those ideas together?

topics.ds: Describe in depth a character, setting, or event in a story or drama, drawing on specific details from the text such as a character's thoughts, words, actions, and interactions
e: Write a detailed character description drawing on evidence from multiple points in the text, including what the character says, does, thinks, and how others respond to them
Describe a setting in depth by citing specific sensory details, figurative language, and mood clues the author provides
Explain how a key event affects the characters and plot development, citing specific textual details about actions, reactions, and consequences
topics.p: After {{name}} reads a chapter where an important event happens, can they write or talk about it in detail — describing what the character thought, said, and did, using specific words and moments from the text?

topics.ds: Interpret information presented visually, orally, or quantitatively in informational texts (e.g., charts, graphs, diagrams, timelines, animations) and explain how it contributes to understanding the text
e: Read and interpret data from a chart, graph, or table included in an informational text and explain how it supports or extends the written information
Explain how a diagram, map, or timeline in an informational text helps the reader understand the topic in ways that words alone might not
Synthesise information from both the written text and a visual element (graph, illustration, infographic) to draw a conclusion that neither source provides independently
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a non-fiction article that includes a chart or timeline, can they explain what extra information those visuals add — beyond what the written text says?

topics.ds: Identify the purpose of layout features in print and digital texts (headings, columns, banners, sidebars, text boxes, icons) and the words used for navigation such as home, back, menu, search and next
e: Explain what the home, back, menu and search buttons do on a children's website and use each one
Compare the layout of a printed magazine page with a web page on the same topic and say what each layout feature (banner, sidebar, text box) is for
Type a keyword into a website's search box to find a page and explain why they chose that word
topics.p: On a website, does {{name}} know what 'home', 'back', 'menu' and 'search' do — and use them to find what they need?

topics.n: Morals in Fables, Folktales and Myths
topics.ds: Explain how the central message, lesson, or moral of a story is conveyed through key details across diverse text types including fables, folktales, and myths
e: Retell a fable and identify the moral, citing three key details that convey it
Compare how two myths from different cultures convey a similar central message through different events
Explain the difference between the topic of a story and its central message or lesson
topics.p: After reading a myth or folktale from another culture, can {{name}} explain what lesson or value it was teaching — and say which details in the story showed that?

topics.ds: Discuss the effects of literary devices such as rhythm and onomatopoeia in poetry and prose: how they enhance meaning and shape the reader's reaction
e: Find onomatopoeia in a poem or story (e.g. 'crash', 'sizzle', 'drip') and explain how it helps the reader hear the scene
Read aloud a poem with a fast rhythm and one with a slow rhythm and describe how each makes the reader feel
Explain how short, rhythmic sentences in a prose action scene (e.g. 'Run. Jump. Splash!') build excitement
topics.p: When reading a poem or story with 'sound words' like 'crash' or 'sizzle', can {{name}} explain how they help them hear or feel what's happening?

topics.ds: Recognise how texts with similar purposes are created differently for different audiences, by comparing word choice, sentence length, images and layout
e: Compare two information texts about volcanoes, one for young children and one for adults, and list the differences in words and pictures
Explain how an invitation to a friend's party differs from an invitation to a school assembly for parents
Identify who each of two ads for the same product is aimed at and point to the features that show it
topics.p: If {{name}} sees two ads or books on the same topic — one for little kids and one for grown-ups — can they spot how they're written differently?

topics.ds: Discuss characters, events and settings in different contexts (places, times, cultures) in literature by First Nations Australian, other Australian and world authors and illustrators
e: Discuss how the setting and events of a First Nations Australian story (e.g. 'Shake a Leg' by Boori Monty Pryor and Jan Ormerod) connect to culture and Country
Compare the setting and events of an Australian story set in the bush (e.g. Jackie French's 'Diary of a Wombat') with those of a story set in a city
Explain how a character's actions make sense in their story's context (e.g. a different place or time) using details from the text
topics.p: When reading a story set somewhere very different — the outback, a big city, or long ago — can {{name}} explain how the place and time shape what happens to the characters?

topics.ds: Use structural terminology (chapter, scene, stanza) to refer to parts of literary texts and describe how each successive part builds on earlier sections
e: Identify chapters, scenes, or stanzas in a given text and use the correct term for each
Explain how the second stanza of a poem builds on the mood established in the first
Describe how a specific chapter advances the plot by referring to events in earlier chapters
topics.p: When {{name}} talks about a book they're reading, do they use words like "chapter", "stanza", or "scene" correctly — and can they explain how a later chapter builds on what happened earlier?

topics.ds: Describe the overall structure of an informational text (chronology, comparison, cause/effect, problem/solution) and explain how the author's chosen structure helps convey information and ideas
e: Identify which organisational structure an informational text uses (chronological order, compare/contrast, cause/effect, or problem/solution) and cite textual features that signal it
Explain how signal words (first, then, finally for chronology; however, similarly for comparison; because, as a result for cause/effect; the solution was for problem/solution) reveal text structure
Compare two informational texts on the same topic that use different structures and explain how each structure affects the way information is presented to the reader
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a non-fiction text, can they identify how it's organised — for example, "this one is structured as a problem and solution" or "this one goes through events in time order" — and explain why that structure works?

topics.ds: Compare and contrast the treatment of similar themes, topics, and story patterns (e.g., good vs evil, quest narratives, trickster tales) in stories, myths, and traditional literature from different cultures
e: Compare how two myths or folk tales from different cultures treat a similar theme (e.g., creation, heroism, the importance of honesty) and explain both similarities and differences
Identify recurring story patterns across cultures such as the trickster figure, the quest, or the transformation, providing specific examples from texts read
Explain how cultural context shapes the way a universal theme is expressed differently in stories from various traditions
topics.p: If {{name}} has read two quest stories from different cultures — like a Greek myth and a West African folktale — can they compare how each treats the hero's journey and what values each story prizes?

topics.ds: Use comprehension strategies when listening to and viewing texts (films, videos, podcasts, multimodal texts) to build literal and inferred meaning, and begin to evaluate texts using knowledge of context, structure and language features
e: Watch a short animated film and answer literal questions (who, where, what happened) and an inference question (why a character acted that way)
Use clues from music, camera close-ups and characters' expressions in a video to infer how a character feels
Give an opinion of a short documentary or podcast episode (e.g. 'It explained clearly because...') using one feature of its structure or language as evidence
topics.p: After watching a short film or kids' documentary, can {{name}} tell you what happened, why a character acted that way, and whether they thought it was good — with a reason?

topics.ds: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as used in literary texts, including understanding references to mythology and cultural allusions (e.g., Herculean, Achilles' heel)
e: Explain the meaning of an allusion drawn from mythology when encountered in a text, e.g. identify that 'Herculean task' means an extremely difficult task, referencing Hercules' legendary labours
Use context and knowledge of word parts to determine the meaning of unfamiliar words in a poem or story, explaining how the word contributes to tone or meaning
Identify when an author is using a word figuratively rather than literally and explain the intended meaning in context
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a story that mentions something like "a Herculean task" or "an Achilles heel", can they work out what it means — or look it up and explain the mythological reference behind it?

topics.ds: Explain events, procedures, ideas, or concepts in an informational text, including what happened and why, by citing specific textual evidence about causes, effects, and steps in a process
e: Explain a historical event described in an informational text by identifying both what happened and the causes leading to it, using specific details from the text
Describe the steps in a procedure or process presented in an informational text, explaining why each step is necessary based on information in the text
Identify cause-and-effect relationships between ideas or events in an informational passage and explain them using evidence from the text
topics.p: After reading a non-fiction article that explains how something works — like how volcanoes form — can {{name}} write down the main steps or causes in their own words, citing the specific evidence the author used?

topics.ds: Distinguish between statements of fact and statements of opinion in texts, recognising how authors blend factual information with subjective viewpoints
e: Identify and label statements as fact or opinion in a newspaper article
Explain why a statement is a fact by citing verifiable evidence or why it is an opinion
Recognise persuasive techniques that present opinions as if they were facts
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a newspaper article or non-fiction text, can they point out which parts are facts and which parts are the author's opinions — and explain how they can tell the difference?

topics.ds: Determine the theme of a story, drama, or poem from details in the text, and provide an objective summary that captures the key events without personal opinions
e: Identify the theme of a story (e.g. courage, friendship, overcoming adversity) by examining what characters learn, how they change, and what the author emphasises across the whole text
Distinguish theme from topic: explain that a topic might be 'war' while the theme is 'the cost of conflict on families'
Summarise a story, chapter, or poem objectively, including only key events and details without inserting personal opinions or minor details
topics.p: After reading a novel or a poem, can {{name}} explain the theme — like "it's about not giving up" — and then write a brief summary of the plot without mixing it up with their own opinions?

topics.ds: Compare and contrast a firsthand account (autobiography, diary, letter) with a secondhand account (biography, textbook, news report) of the same event or topic, identifying differences in focus and information provided
e: Explain the difference between a firsthand account (written by someone who experienced the event) and a secondhand account (written by someone who researched it), using specific examples
Compare a diary entry and a textbook passage about the same historical event, identifying what each account includes, omits, and emphasises
Analyse how the perspective of the writer (participant vs observer/researcher) affects the information provided, the language used, and the overall tone
topics.p: If {{name}} reads both a diary entry by someone who was at a historical event and a textbook account of the same event, can they explain what's different about the two — like what details each one includes and why?

topics.ds: Identify text navigation features of online texts that enhance readability, including headlines, drop-down menus, links, graphics and layout, and explain how each helps the reader
e: Use the headline, menu and hyperlinks of a children's news website to find a story and explain how each feature helped
Compare a cluttered and a clear web page on the same topic and explain which layout and graphics make it easier to read
Explain how a link's words (e.g. 'Find out more about turtles') tell the reader where it goes
topics.p: When reading a kids' news site, can {{name}} use the headlines, menus and links to find a story — and say what makes one website easier to read than another?

topics.ds: Explain how an author of an informational text uses reasons and evidence to support particular points, evaluating whether the reasoning is sound and the evidence is relevant and sufficient
e: Identify the key points an author makes in an informational text and list the specific reasons and evidence provided to support each point
Evaluate whether the evidence an author uses (facts, statistics, examples, expert opinions) is relevant to the point being made and sufficient to be convincing
Distinguish between well-supported claims backed by evidence and unsupported opinions or assertions in an informational text
topics.p: After reading a persuasive article — like one arguing for or against something — can {{name}} identify the reasons the author gives and say whether each one is convincing and well-supported?

topics.ds: Explore the effect of choices in framing (close-up, mid shot, long shot), placement of elements and salience (what stands out through size, colour, light or position) on the composition of still and moving images in texts
e: Compare a close-up and a long shot of the same character in a picture book or film and explain how each makes the viewer feel
Identify the most salient element in an illustration or poster (e.g. the brightest or largest object) and explain why the creator made it stand out
Rearrange the elements of a simple photo or drawing on a tablet (e.g. move the main subject from the centre to the edge) and describe how the meaning changes
topics.p: When looking at a picture book or a movie scene, can {{name}} explain why the illustrator zoomed in close, or made one thing bigger or brighter than the rest?

topics.n: How Language Choices Affect the Reader
topics.ds: Evaluate how authors use language including figurative language, considering the impact of word choices, imagery, and literary devices on the reader
e: Explain how a specific metaphor or simile affects the reader's understanding or emotions
Evaluate an author's choice of descriptive language and its impact on atmosphere
Compare how different authors use figurative language to achieve similar effects
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a descriptive passage with figurative language — like "the sun was a burning eye" — can they explain what image or feeling the author was creating and whether it was effective?

topics.n: How Parts Build a Whole Text
topics.ds: Explain how a series of chapters, scenes, or stanzas fits together to provide the overall structure of a story, drama, or poem, analysing how each part contributes to the whole
e: Map the structure of a novel showing how each chapter advances plot or character development
Explain how individual stanzas in a poem build toward a central theme or message
Analyse how scenes in a play work together to develop conflict and resolution
topics.p: After finishing a novel, can {{name}} explain how each chapter contributed to the whole — like how an early chapter introduced a tension that wasn't resolved until much later?

topics.ds: Provide reasoned justifications for views about texts, supporting interpretations and opinions with evidence and logical arguments
e: State an opinion about a character's motivations and support it with three pieces of textual evidence
Construct a reasoned argument about an author's message using quotes from the text
Respond to an alternative interpretation by providing counter-evidence from the text
topics.p: When {{name}} shares an opinion about a book — like "I think the villain had a point" — can they back it up with specific quotes or events from the text, rather than just saying how they feel?

topics.ds: Analyse multiple accounts of the same event or topic, noting important similarities and differences in the point of view they represent
e: Compare two news articles about the same event and identify differences in perspective
Explain how the author's background or purpose affects their account of an event
Identify which facts are consistent across accounts and which details differ based on viewpoint
topics.p: If {{name}} reads two different accounts of the same event — like two news articles covering the same story — can they explain what each account emphasises, what each leaves out, and why the perspectives differ?

topics.ds: Compare and contrast the point of view from which different stories are narrated, including distinguishing between first-person and third-person narration and explaining how the narrator's perspective shapes the reader's understanding
e: Identify whether a story is told in first person (I/we) or third person (he/she/they) and explain how this affects what the reader knows about characters' thoughts and feelings
Compare two versions of a story or event told from different points of view and explain how each narrator's perspective changes what is emphasised, omitted, or revealed
Explain why an author might choose first-person narration (immediacy, personal voice) versus third-person narration (broader view, objectivity) for a particular story
topics.p: After reading a story written in first person, can {{name}} explain how the story might feel different if it were told by a different character or by a narrator watching from the outside?

topics.ds: Compare texts from different times with similar purposes and audiences (e.g. an older and a modern news report, school reader or advertisement) to identify similarities and differences in how they depict events
e: Compare a 1950s and a modern newspaper report about a flood and list differences in language, images and what is included
Compare an old school reader with a modern picture book on the same topic and describe how families or children are shown differently
Explain one reason the older text might depict the event differently (e.g. different technology or attitudes at the time)
topics.p: If {{name}} looks at an old newspaper or ad and a modern one about the same kind of thing, can they spot how the language and pictures have changed?

topics.ds: Explain major differences between poems, drama, and prose, identifying structural elements unique to each form: verse, rhythm, and meter in poetry; cast of characters, dialogue, and stage directions in drama; chapters and paragraphs in prose
e: Compare a poem, a play script, and a prose passage on a similar theme, identifying the structural features unique to each form (e.g. stanzas vs scenes vs chapters)
Identify and explain the function of structural elements in drama: cast list, stage directions (in italics or brackets), dialogue format, and scene divisions
Describe how structural elements of poetry such as verse, rhythm, meter, and line breaks affect how a poem is read aloud and how meaning is conveyed
topics.p: Can {{name}} look at a poem, a play, and a chapter from a novel and explain how each is laid out differently — for example, that a play has stage directions and a poem has verses?

topics.ds: Examine the use of literary devices and deliberate word play in literary texts, including poetry, to shape meaning: puns, invented words, double meanings and nonsense verse
e: Explain the double meaning in a pun (e.g. 'The bicycle couldn't stand up because it was two-tired')
Find invented words in a nonsense poem (e.g. C. J. Dennis's 'The Triantiwontigongolope' or Lewis Carroll's 'Jabberwocky') and work out what they might mean
Explain how an author uses word play in a humorous book (e.g. Andy Griffiths' 'The 13-Storey Treehouse') to make the reader laugh
topics.p: Does {{name}} get the joke in a pun or a silly made-up word in a poem — and can they explain the double meaning?

topics.ds: Recommend books to peers, giving reasons for choices based on knowledge of a wide range of genres, authors, and themes, and making comparisons within and across books
e: Recommend a book to a peer by explaining its genre, theme, and what makes it engaging, comparing it to other books the peer has enjoyed
Justify a book recommendation by referring to specific features such as the author's style, the plot structure, or how a theme is developed
Maintain a reading log or book review collection that captures key responses to books read and serves as a reference for future recommendations
topics.p: When {{name}} recommends a book to a friend, can they explain clearly why they think that person would enjoy it — mentioning the genre, characters, and themes rather than just saying "it's good"?

topics.ds: Recognise similar storylines, ideas and relationships in different contexts in literary texts by First Nations Australian, other Australian and world authors
e: Compare how a published Dreaming story by a First Nations Australian author-illustrator (e.g. Dick Roughsey's 'The Rainbow Serpent', in which Goorialla's journey forms the rivers and ranges) and a creation story from another culture each explain how features of the land came to be, citing events from both texts
Identify the quest storyline in an Australian novel (e.g. Emily Rodda's 'Rowan of Rin') and in a world story, and describe how their contexts differ
Explain how a friendship or family relationship is similar in two stories set in different places, quoting a line from each that shows it
topics.p: When reading, does {{name}} notice when two stories from different places — like an Australian story and a fairytale from overseas — have a similar plot or message?

topics.ds: Identify how texts across the curriculum have different language features and are typically organised into characteristic stages depending on purpose (e.g. procedure: goal, materials, steps; explanation: phenomenon, sequence of causes; report: classification, description; recount: orientation, events, reorientation)
e: Label the stages of a science explanation (e.g. how rain forms) and name the cause-and-effect language used
Label the stages of a procedure and of a historical recount and explain how their language features differ (command verbs vs past tense and time connectives)
Choose the right text type and stages for a task in another subject (e.g. reporting on an animal in science) and explain the choice
topics.p: When {{name}} writes for science or history, do they know how that kind of text is usually set out — like the steps of an experiment or the stages of a recount?

topics.ds: Make connections between the text of a story or drama and a visual or oral presentation of the text, identifying where each version reflects specific descriptions and directions from the text
e: Compare a passage from a book with a film or audio adaptation, identifying specific moments where the visual or oral version matches or departs from the written text
Explain how a film, illustration, or dramatic performance interprets a scene from a story, citing specific textual descriptions the adaptation reflects
Identify details in the written text (descriptions of setting, character appearance, dialogue) that a visual or oral presentation brings to life, and note any differences
topics.p: If {{name}} has read a book and then seen a film version, can they compare the two — pointing out moments where the film showed something differently from how the book described it?

topics.ds: Use visualising together with other comprehension strategies to build literal and inferred meaning, expand topic knowledge and evaluate texts
e: Draw or describe a setting from a chapter without pictures and annotate it with the phrases from the text that created the image
Use a visualisation to infer mood or a character's feelings (e.g. 'I picture her hunched over, so she must be scared')
Compare their visualisation with a film or illustrated version and evaluate which matches the text more closely, giving evidence
topics.p: After reading a chapter, can {{name}} describe the scene they pictured — using the author's words — and say whether the movie version matched the book?

topics.ds: Make comparisons within and across books, identifying similarities and differences in themes, characters, settings, and authorial choices across multiple texts
e: Compare how two authors develop similar themes using different narrative techniques
Identify similarities and differences between characters across books by the same author
Analyse how settings function differently in two texts from the same genre
topics.p: After reading a few books by the same author or in the same genre, can {{name}} compare them — discussing what themes, styles, or character types the author tends to use?

topics.ds: Compare and contrast two or more characters, settings, or events in a story or drama, drawing on specific details about how characters interact, settings influence action, or events connect
e: Create a Venn diagram comparing two characters' traits using textual evidence
Explain how a change in setting affects the mood and characters' actions in a story
Analyse how two events in a narrative are connected through cause and effect
topics.p: After reading a novel with several main characters, can {{name}} compare two of them in detail — explaining how their personalities, experiences, and relationships are both similar and different?

topics.ds: Compare and contrast the overall structure of events, ideas, concepts, or information in two or more informational texts, identifying patterns such as chronology, comparison, cause/effect, or problem/solution
e: Identify the organisational structure of two texts on the same topic
Explain how one text uses cause/effect while another uses problem/solution to present information
Analyse why an author chose a particular structure for their informational text
topics.p: If {{name}} reads two non-fiction texts about the same topic that are organised differently — one in time order and one comparing two sides — can they describe those structural differences and explain how each one shapes the reader's experience?

topics.ds: Describe how a narrator's or speaker's point of view influences how events are described, recognising the difference between limited and omniscient narration and how perspective shapes storytelling
e: Identify whether a story uses first-person or third-person narration and explain the effect
Explain how events would be described differently if told from another character's perspective
Analyse how the narrator's knowledge or bias affects what information the reader receives
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain how a story told by an all-knowing narrator feels different from one told by a single character who only knows their own side — and give an example of how that changes what the reader knows?

topics.ds: Explain the relationships or interactions between two or more individuals, events, ideas, or concepts in historical, scientific, or technical texts based on specific information
e: Explain the cause-and-effect relationship between events in a historical text
Describe how a scientific process involves sequential steps that depend on each other
Identify how key individuals in a text influenced events or other people
topics.p: After reading a history or science text about how two events or discoveries were connected, can {{name}} explain that relationship clearly — describing how one thing led to or influenced the other?

topics.ds: Compare and contrast stories in the same genre on their approaches to similar themes and topics, identifying how different authors treat common ideas
e: Compare how two mystery stories create suspense using different techniques
Identify common themes in adventure stories and explain how each author develops them differently
Analyse how two authors from the same genre approach the theme of friendship or courage
topics.p: After reading two adventure stories in the same genre, can {{name}} compare how each author handled similar elements — like the hero's challenge or the resolution — and say which approach they preferred and why?

topics.ds: Explain how the sequence of images in print, digital and film texts (picture-book spreads, comic panels, slideshow images, film shots) affects meaning, pacing and the reader's or viewer's response
e: Rearrange the panels of a short comic strip and explain how the new order changes the story or joke
Explain how a sequence of shots in a film scene (e.g. a long shot followed by a close-up) builds tension or reveals information
Explain how the order of images in a wordless or nearly wordless book (e.g. Shaun Tan's 'The Arrival') leads the viewer to an idea
topics.p: When reading a comic or watching a movie scene, can {{name}} explain how the order of the pictures or shots builds suspense or tells the story?

topics.ds: Analyse how visual and multimedia elements contribute to the meaning, tone, or beauty of a text such as graphic novels, multimedia presentations, or illustrated editions of fiction and poetry
e: Explain how illustrations in a graphic novel convey emotion or advance the story
Analyse how visual elements such as colour and layout affect the tone of a multimedia text
Compare how the same scene is portrayed in text versus in visual or audio format
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a graphic novel or illustrated book, can they explain how the pictures and layout — not just the words — help tell the story or create a particular mood?

topics.ds: Examine the effects of imagery, including simile, metaphor and personification, and of sound devices such as alliteration, assonance, onomatopoeia and rhyme in narratives, poetry and songs
e: Identify personification in a poem or story (e.g. 'The wind howled at the door') and explain the image and feeling it creates
Find alliteration and assonance in a song or poem (e.g. 'the slow, low moan of the sea') and explain how the sounds affect the mood
Compare the effect of onomatopoeia in a narrative action scene with the effect of rhyme in a song lyric
topics.p: When listening to a song or poem, can {{name}} notice when the writer makes the wind 'howl' like a person, or repeats sounds — and say what feeling that creates?

topics.ds: Quote accurately from literary and informational texts when explaining what the text says explicitly and when drawing inferences, using quotation marks and citations correctly
e: Select and copy exact words from a text to support an inference about character motivation
Use quotation marks correctly when incorporating textual evidence into written responses
Introduce quotes with signal phrases such as 'The author states' or 'According to the text'
topics.p: When {{name}} writes about a book or article for school, do they quote from the text directly — putting the exact words in speech marks — to support their points?

topics.ds: Identify aspects of literary texts that represent details or information about historical, social and cultural contexts, in literature by First Nations Australian, other Australian and world authors
e: Identify details in a First Nations Australian verse novel or story (e.g. Sally Morgan's 'Sister Heart') that show the historical and social context of the Stolen Generations, and discuss them respectfully
List details of daily life in different decades shown in an Australian text (e.g. Nadia Wheatley and Donna Rawlins' 'My Place') and explain what each reveals about that time
Explain how a world author's novel shows the cultural customs or social rules of its setting, citing two details
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a story set in the past or in another culture, can they point out the details — clothes, jobs, rules, events — that show what life was like then and there?

topics.ds: Navigate and read texts for specific purposes, monitoring meaning using the strategies of skimming (for gist), scanning (for specific details) and confirming (re-reading to check information)
e: Skim an article for 30 seconds using its headings and first sentences, then state its main idea
Scan a timetable, index or web page for a specific date, name or keyword and locate it quickly
Confirm an answer by returning to the relevant section, re-reading it closely and correcting the answer if needed
topics.p: When {{name}} needs a fact for homework, can they quickly skim a page for the main idea, scan for the exact detail, and then re-read to check they got it right?

topics.ds: Describe how spoken, written and multimodal texts use language features and are organised into characteristic stages and phases depending on purpose (e.g. a speech's introduction, points and conclusion; a documentary's hook, explanation and summary; a podcast interview's introduction, questions and sign-off)
e: Identify the stages of a persuasive speech (position, arguments, restated position) in a video recording and the language features of each stage
Map the stages and phases of a short documentary or explainer video (hook, information segments, summary) and note how images and narration work together in each
Compare the stages of a written recount with those of a spoken or podcast recount of the same event and explain the differences in language
topics.p: When watching a kids' documentary or listening to a podcast, can {{name}} notice how it's structured — the hook at the start, the main parts, and the wrap-up?

topics.ds: Determine two or more main ideas of an informational text and explain how they are supported by key details, then summarise the text without personal opinions
e: Identify the main ideas in each section of an informational article
List key details that support each main idea in a multi-paragraph text
Write an objective summary capturing the main ideas without adding personal opinions
topics.p: After reading a long non-fiction article, can {{name}} identify two or three main ideas it covers and write a brief summary that captures all of them — without adding their own opinions?

topics.ds: Explain how an author uses reasons and evidence to support particular points in a text, identifying which reasons and evidence support which specific points
e: Match each of an author's main points with the evidence used to support it
Evaluate whether the evidence provided adequately supports the author's argument
Identify points in a text that lack sufficient evidence or reasoning
topics.p: After reading a persuasive text, can {{name}} map out which reasons the author uses to support which specific points — showing that they understand the structure of the argument, not just the conclusion?

topics.ds: Integrate information from several texts on the same topic in order to write or speak about the subject knowledgeably, combining information without plagiarising
e: Combine information from three sources into a coherent paragraph using own words
Create a fact sheet that synthesises key information from multiple texts on one topic
Present information orally that draws on multiple sources while crediting the sources
topics.p: When {{name}} writes a school report using several sources, do they bring together information from all of them into their own words — rather than just quoting or copying from one source at a time?

topics.ds: Describe the ways in which a text reflects the time and place in which it was created, through its language, values, references, technology and images
e: Identify words, references and attitudes in an older Australian story or poem (e.g. a Banjo Paterson ballad) that show when and where it was written
Compare a 1980s and a recent advertisement for the same type of product and explain what each reveals about its time
Explain how a modern Australian picture book reflects present-day concerns (e.g. sustainability or diverse families)
topics.p: When {{name}} reads an old poem or watches an old ad, can they spot the clues — words, ideas or technology — that show when and where it was made?

topics.ds: Draw on information from multiple print or digital sources, demonstrating the ability to locate an answer to a question quickly or solve a problem efficiently
e: Use search features, indexes, and headings to locate specific information across sources
Synthesise information from two or more sources to answer a research question
Evaluate which source provides the most relevant information for a given question
topics.p: When {{name}} needs to answer a research question for school, can they search across several books or websites to find the relevant information quickly — rather than reading every source from start to finish?

topics.ds: Use visualising with other comprehension strategies to build literal and inferred meaning from complex literary and informative texts, to evaluate information and ideas, and to connect and compare content across sources
e: Visualise a process described in an informative text (e.g. the water cycle) and sketch a labelled diagram to check their understanding
Use the sensory details in a descriptive passage to describe their mental image and explain how it helps them infer mood or theme
Compare the mental pictures built from two sources on the same topic (e.g. a poem and a documentary about a bushfire) and evaluate which gives the clearer or more accurate picture
topics.p: When {{name}} reads about something complicated — like how a volcano erupts — can they picture it in their head or sketch it to check they understand?

topics.ds: Analyse how a text's structure — including its overall organisation, use of chapters, stanzas, scenes, paragraphs, or sections — contributes to its meaning, style, and development of ideas
e: Explain how a non-chronological structure (e.g., flashback, frame narrative) creates suspense or surprise
Analyse the role of a specific paragraph in developing and refining a key concept in a non-fiction text
Compare how two texts use different structures (e.g., epistolary vs. linear narrative) and the effect of each
topics.p: When {{name}} analyses a poem or novel, can they explain how the author's structural choices — like starting in the middle of the action, or ending with a repeated image — shape the overall meaning of the text?

topics.ds: Explain how texts across the curriculum are organised into characteristic stages and phases depending on purpose, and recognise how authors adapt or blend text structures and language features (e.g. a narrative used to inform in science, a persuasive information text, a historical diary used to recount)
e: Identify the information-report stages and narrative features blended in a science text told as a story (e.g. a day in the life of a water droplet)
Analyse a hybrid persuasive-information text (e.g. an environmental campaign web page) and explain which stages inform and which persuade
Explain why an author adapted a familiar structure for a purpose in another learning area, such as a diary used to recount a historical event
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a science book written like a story, or a campaign website that mixes facts and persuasion, can they explain how the author blended text types — and why?

topics.ds: Make critical comparisons across texts — comparing themes, characters, settings, styles, or arguments in two or more works, including texts from different periods, genres, or cultures
e: Compare how two novels treat a shared theme (e.g., growing up) using specific evidence from both
Analyse how a modern retelling draws on and transforms elements from a traditional story or myth
Compare conflicting accounts of the same event in two non-fiction texts and evaluate which is more convincing
topics.p: After reading texts from very different times or cultures, can {{name}} compare them thoughtfully — noting not just surface similarities but deeper differences in values, style, and what the author assumed about their reader?

topics.ds: Evaluate arguments and claims in non-fiction texts — assess whether reasoning is sound, evidence is relevant and sufficient, distinguish between fact and opinion, and recognise bias, propaganda, and rhetorical techniques
e: Identify the main claim in an argument text and evaluate whether the evidence presented is sufficient
Spot logical fallacies or irrelevant evidence introduced to distract from weak reasoning
Compare two opposing arguments on the same issue and evaluate which is more convincing, with reasons
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a persuasive piece — like an editorial or a speech — can they identify the rhetorical techniques being used, evaluate whether the argument is logically sound, and explain what might be biased or misleading?

topics.ds: Determine the meaning of figurative and connotative language in context, analyse the impact of specific word choices on meaning and tone, and identify literary devices such as metaphor, simile, personification, allusion, and irony
e: Identify a metaphor or simile in a passage and explain its effect on the reader
Explain how an author's word choice creates a particular tone (e.g., menacing, humorous, melancholic)
Recognise an allusion to a myth, the Bible, or another text and explain what it adds to the meaning
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a passage containing a metaphor, irony, or allusion, can they explain what the author really meant — going beyond the literal words to describe the effect that device creates for the reader?

topics.ds: Identify responses to characters and events in literary texts that are drawn from historical, social or cultural contexts, in literature by First Nations Australian, other Australian and world authors, including how readers' own contexts shape their responses
e: Explain how the historical context of colonisation shapes readers' responses to events in an allegorical Australian picture book (e.g. 'The Rabbits' by John Marsden and Shaun Tan)
Discuss how a First Nations Australian author's verse novel (e.g. Kirli Saunders' 'Bindi') invites responses to characters and events shaped by culture and Country
Compare their own response to a character with that of a reader from a different time or culture and explain the difference
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a story about the past or another culture, can they explain why people from different backgrounds might feel differently about a character or event?

topics.ds: Examine texts, including media texts (news reports, ads, social media posts, documentaries), that represent ideas and events, and identify how they reflect the context — time, place, culture and audience — in which they were created
e: Compare news coverage of the same kind of event from two different decades or countries and explain how each reflects its context
Identify the values and assumptions about the audience in a current advertisement or social media campaign
Explain how a documentary's choice of interviewees and images reflects when, where and for whom it was made
topics.p: When watching the news or an ad, can {{name}} explain how it reflects the time, place and people it was made for — and how it might look different elsewhere?

topics.ds: Analyse point of view and narrative perspective — including first person, third person limited and omniscient, and unreliable narrator — and how the author's or narrator's perspective shapes the reader's understanding and creates effects such as suspense, irony, or humour
e: Identify the narrative perspective of a text and explain how it limits or expands the reader's knowledge
Explain how dramatic irony arises when the reader knows something a character does not
Compare how the same event might be told differently from two characters' perspectives
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a story with an unreliable narrator — where the person telling the story isn't fully trustworthy — can they spot the clues that suggest the narrator isn't giving the full picture?

topics.ds: Analyse how plot structure unfolds through episodes or key events, and how characters develop, respond to challenges, and change over the course of a narrative — including the relationship between character, setting, and plot
e: Trace how a character's attitude changes across a story and identify the turning points
Explain how a specific incident in a drama propels the action or provokes a decision
Analyse how the setting influences a character's behaviour or the mood of a scene
topics.p: After reading a novel, can {{name}} explain how the main character changed from the beginning to the end — pointing to specific events that caused that change and how the setting shaped who they became?

topics.ds: Recognise and understand poetic conventions — including form (sonnet, ballad, free verse), metre, rhyme scheme, stanza structure, imagery, and sound devices (alliteration, assonance, onomatopoeia) — and analyse how poets use them for effect
e: Identify the form of a poem (e.g., sonnet, haiku, ballad) and explain its key structural features
Analyse how a poet uses rhythm or sound devices to reinforce meaning or mood
Explain how enjambment or a caesura affects the pace and emphasis of a line
topics.p: When {{name}} reads a poem, can they identify its form — like a sonnet or a ballad — and explain how the poet's use of rhyme, rhythm, and imagery contributes to the poem's meaning or emotional impact?

topics.ds: Identify the purpose, audience, and context of a text and use this knowledge to support comprehension — recognising how writing aimed at different audiences (academic, popular, persuasive) uses different conventions, register, and tone
e: Identify the intended audience and purpose of a text and explain how the language choices reflect this
Compare a newspaper article and a scientific report on the same topic, noting differences in register and structure
Explain how knowing the historical or social context of a text deepens understanding
topics.p: When {{name}} reads something written for a very different audience — like a scientific journal article versus a children's book on the same topic — can they explain how the purpose and audience shaped the language, tone, and structure?

topics.ds: Identify and explain the characteristics that define an author's individual style — recurring themes, sentence patterns, vocabulary, humour, narrative voice, structures such as twist endings, and illustration style
e: Read three stories by one author (e.g. Paul Jennings' short stories) and list recurring features such as twist endings and humour
Explain with examples how an author-illustrator's visual and written style is recognisable across books (e.g. Shaun Tan's surreal images and sparse text)
Write a short paragraph in the style of a studied author and explain which style features they imitated
topics.p: After reading several books by a favourite author, can {{name}} describe what makes that author's writing recognisable — like their twist endings or kind of humour?

topics.ds: Explain the way authors use sound devices (alliteration, assonance, rhythm, rhyme, onomatopoeia) together with imagery to create meaning and effect in poetry
e: Explain how the rhythm and rhyme of an Australian ballad (e.g. Banjo Paterson's 'The Man from Snowy River') create a sense of galloping speed
Explain how assonance and alliteration combine with imagery in a poem to create a particular mood (e.g. calm, menace or joy)
Read a poem aloud twice — once flatly and once stressing its sound devices — and explain how the meaning and effect change
topics.p: When reading a poem aloud, can {{name}} explain how its rhythm and repeated sounds help create a feeling — like the galloping beat of a horse-riding poem?

topics.ds: Determine and analyse the theme or central idea of a text, trace how it develops across the text through key details and events, and provide an objective summary distinct from personal opinion
e: Identify a theme in a novel and explain how specific events develop it across the plot
Distinguish between the topic of a text (what it is about) and the theme (what it is saying)
Write a concise, objective summary of a chapter or article without inserting personal opinion
topics.p: After reading a novel or long poem, can {{name}} explain what it was really about at its deepest level — the central idea or theme — and trace how that idea developed through key moments in the text?
