Create a bibliography listing sources used in a research project
Paraphrase key information from a source without changing the meaning
topics.p: If {{name}} is researching a topic for a school project, can they find information from books or websites, put it in their own words, and keep track of where they got it from?

topics.ds: Plan, create, edit and publish digital multimodal texts (e.g. slideshows, e-books, web pages, short videos) that combine paragraphs with images, captions, diagrams or graphs, layout and audio, choosing each visual and digital feature to suit purpose and audience
e: Create a slideshow or e-book on a research topic combining paragraphs with images, captions and a diagram or graph
Edit the layout, headings, image placement and font in a digital tool to make the text clearer for a younger audience, explaining each change
Add recorded narration or a hyperlink to the multimodal text and explain how each visual or digital feature supports its purpose
topics.p: Could {{name}} create a slideshow or short e-book on a topic — with writing, images, captions and maybe a voice recording — and explain why they laid it out that way?

topics.n: Layout and Formatting in Informational Writing

Present comparative information using a table with clear row and column headers
Use columns and bullet points to display information in a scannable format
topics.p: When {{name}} writes a non-fiction piece — like a guide or an explanation — do they use layout features like headings, bullet points, and columns to help the reader navigate the information easily?

topics.ds: Plan narrative writing by considering how authors have developed characters and settings, drawing on techniques observed in texts read, heard, or performed

Plan a character using techniques such as showing through action borrowed from a studied author
Analyse how an author builds setting and apply similar techniques in planning own narrative
topics.p: When {{name}} is about to write a story, do they think ahead about what their main character is like and where the story will take place before they start writing?

topics.ds: Create and edit literary texts, experimenting with figurative language (simile, metaphor, personification) and with storylines, characters and settings drawn from texts experienced

topics.ds: Precis longer passages by summarising the main ideas and key information concisely while maintaining the essential meaning and removing non-essential detail

Write a precis that is no more than one-third the length of the original text
topics.p: If {{name}} reads a long article about a topic they're studying, can they write a short summary in their own words that captures the key points without copying sentences?

topics.ds: Use varied transitions, cohesive devices, and paragraph-linking strategies to create coherence across a whole piece of writing — including temporal transitions, causal connectives, and techniques for signalling shifts in argument, time, or setting

Signal a shift in time or setting within a narrative using a transitional phrase or paragraph break
Link paragraphs using a cohesive device such as a topic sentence that refers back to the previous paragraph
topics.p: When {{name}} writes several paragraphs, do they use linking phrases like "however," "as a result," or "on the other hand" to connect ideas smoothly between sections?

topics.ds: Write informative and explanatory texts that examine a topic and convey ideas clearly — organising information logically with headings and formatting, developing the topic with relevant facts, definitions, details, and quotations, and using precise vocabulary

Develop a topic using well-chosen facts, definitions, concrete details, and quotations from sources
Use domain-specific vocabulary and formatting (headings, graphics) to aid the reader's comprehension
topics.p: Can {{name}} write a clear explanation of how something works — like how a volcano erupts or how bread is made — so that someone who's never learned about it would understand?

topics.ds: Create and edit literary texts that adapt plot structure, characters, settings and/or ideas from texts experienced, experimenting with literary devices such as flashback, foreshadowing, figurative language and symbolism

Edit a draft to strengthen one literary device and annotate the change and its intended effect on the reader
topics.p: When {{name}} writes a story, do they experiment with tricks like a flashback to a character's past, or an early hint about what's coming?

topics.ds: Write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence — including introducing claims, acknowledging counterclaims, organising reasons logically, maintaining a formal style, and providing a concluding statement

Acknowledge and respond to a counterclaim rather than ignoring opposing views
Use linking words and phrases (however, furthermore, consequently) to connect claims, reasons, and evidence

topics.ds: Plan, revise, and edit writing to improve coherence and effectiveness — considering how the writing reflects its intended audience and purpose, amending vocabulary, grammar, and structure, and proofreading for accurate spelling, punctuation, and grammar

Edit sentence-level issues including word choice, grammar, and punctuation before finalising
Reflect on whether the writing achieves its intended effect on the target audience and adjust accordingly
topics.p: After {{name}} finishes a first draft, do they go back and make real improvements — not just fixing spelling, but changing sentences or reorganising ideas to make it better?

topics.ds: Summarise and organise material from reading and research — gathering relevant information from multiple sources, assessing credibility, integrating evidence without plagiarising, and supporting ideas with factual detail

Paraphrase information from a source accurately without copying word-for-word
Assess whether a source is credible and relevant before including it in research writing
topics.p: If {{name}} is preparing for a school project, can they gather notes from several sources and organise them into a logical order before they start writing?

topics.ds: Write for a range of purposes and audiences beyond narrative — including scripts, poetry, personal and formal letters, notes for talks, and other forms — selecting the appropriate form, register, and conventions for each

Compose a script with stage directions, character names, and realistic dialogue
Adapt writing style (vocabulary, sentence structure, tone) to suit different audiences and purposes
topics.p: Can {{name}} write in different styles depending on the task — for example, a persuasive letter, a set of instructions, or a diary entry — and make each one sound appropriate?

topics.ds: Write narratives that develop real or imagined experiences using effective technique — including establishing context and point of view, developing characters through dialogue, pacing, and description, using varied transitions, and providing a reflective conclusion

Use dialogue, pacing, and descriptive detail to develop characters and advance the plot
Craft a conclusion that reflects on the narrated events rather than simply ending the action
topics.p: When {{name}} writes a story, do they use techniques like describing feelings, building suspense, or showing dialogue to make it interesting to read?

topics.ds: Apply growing knowledge of vocabulary, grammar, and text structure to writing — drawing on literary and rhetorical devices from reading (e.g., rhetorical questions, tricolon, anaphora, contrast) to enhance impact

Employ varied sentence openings and structures to maintain reader interest across a whole piece
Draw on a literary device encountered in reading and apply it consciously in own writing
